Fawn

FAWN -- from Old English faegnian ('to rejoice, be glad'); unrelated to the baby-deer noun. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To fawn is to give someone exaggerated flattery or admiring attention in order to gain their favor.

At the family reunion, several distant cousins spent the whole afternoon fawning over the one relative who had recently won the lottery.

Worked Example

Every time the district manager visited, the staff would fawn over her, laughing at every joke and rushing to refill her coffee before she even noticed it was low.

Notice fawn doesn't aim at any one specific request -- it's ongoing, exaggerated attention meant to win someone's general goodwill, and it often comes across as servile or a little pathetic to onlookers.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

grovel: to behave in a humble, submissive way to please someone

toady: to flatter someone powerful in a servile, self-serving way

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

snub: to treat someone with cold disregard or disrespect

defy: to openly resist or refuse to respect someone's authority

Where it sits · how low you sink to please someone — toady → fawn → grovel

toady vs. fawn: Toady is milder than fawn: a toadying assistant just agrees with every opinion the boss voices, while fawning pours on heavier, more open flattery and attention.

grovel vs. fawn: Grovel is stronger than fawn: fawning flatters someone to win favor, but groveling abases yourself completely -- like begging forgiveness for ten straight minutes over a broken vase.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — faegn-

root — faegn-: glad, joyful (Old English (faegnian, 'to rejoice'))

Put it together

Put it together: Fawn traces back to an Old English word meaning simply 'to rejoice' or act glad. Over time, that glad, eager display curdled into something less sincere: an exaggerated, ingratiating display of delight aimed at winning someone's favor.

Use the root in a new word: fain

Use the root in a new word: fain: In old poetry, a knight might say he would 'fain' serve his lord -- an archaic word for gladly, from the same root as fawn.

Word Choice

Fawn is ongoing, exaggerated flattery aimed at winning someone's general goodwill, often with a servile or slightly contemptible undertone. Compare Coax, which is goal-directed persuasion toward one specific action. Fans fawn over a celebrity just to bask in her attention; you coax a toddler specifically to get her into the bathtub.
